lessons.plain: A relational database stores data in named tables. Keys identify rows; constraints keep rows valid; logical design maps the ER model into tables and references.
goals: Explain relation, tuple, attribute, domain, degree, and cardinality
Find candidate, primary, and foreign keys
Apply integrity rules to a small database

topics.title: Relation, tuple, attribute, and domain
topics.definition: A relation is a set of rows with named columns. A tuple is one row, an attribute is one column, and a domain is the allowed kind of value for that column.
details: Degree (or arity) counts the attributes. Cardinality counts the tuples currently in the relation.
In the mathematical model, a relation has no duplicate tuples and no meaningful row order. A table display may show an order, but a query needs ORDER BY to request one.
topics.example: STUDENT(sid, name, program) has degree 3. If it currently has 40 students, its cardinality is 40.

topics.title: Keys
topics.definition: A superkey is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a smallest such set. One candidate is chosen as the primary key.
details: A table may have several candidate keys. A composite key contains more than one attribute.
A foreign key in one table points to a key in another table, linking the rows.
topics.example: In ENROLLMENT(sid,cid,term,grade), (sid,cid,term) may be the key if a student can take the same course in different terms.

topics.title: Integrity constraints
topics.definition: An integrity constraint is a rule every valid database state must obey.
details: A domain rule restricts a value's type or range. A key rule prevents duplicate identifiers. Entity integrity says no part of the primary key can be NULL.
Referential integrity says a non-NULL foreign-key value must match an existing referenced key. This prevents orphan rows.
topics.example: If ENROLLMENT.sid refers to STUDENT.sid, a registration for sid=999 is rejected when no student 999 exists.

topics.title: Logical database design: ER model to relations
topics.definition: Logical database design converts a conceptual model into relation schemas with keys and constraints while keeping the real-world meaning clear.
details: Create a relation for each strong entity set and choose its primary key. Include useful components of composite attributes as columns.
For a 1:N relationship, place the key from the one side as a foreign key on the many side. For an M:N relationship, create a bridge relation containing both keys and any relationship attributes.
Represent a weak entity with the owner key plus its partial key. Check that foreign keys and uniqueness rules preserve the original ER constraints.
topics.example: Map STUDENT–ENROLLS–COURSE to STUDENT(sid,name), COURSE(cid,title), and ENROLLMENT(sid,cid,term,grade). ENROLLMENT has foreign keys to both parent tables and a key such as (sid,cid,term).

worked.title: Check whether a registration row is allowed
worked.setup: Student IDs 1 and 2 exist. Course DBMS exists. A registration must use a real student, a real course, and a unique student-course pair.

steps.title: Check the values
steps.body: The ID must be a student number, the course must be a known course, and the grade must be an allowed grade.

steps.title: Check for a duplicate
steps.body: Student 1 can have only one DBMS registration row for this term. A second row for the same pair is not allowed.

steps.title: Check the linked records
steps.body: Student 9 is not in STUDENT, so a DBMS registration for student 9 must be rejected.

worked.answer: A valid row uses allowed values, does not repeat its key, and points to student and course rows that really exist.

lessons.exam: Define relation, tuple, degree, and cardinality. Explain primary and foreign keys and show domain, key, entity, and referential constraints with examples.

lessons.plain: Relational algebra builds a query from small table operations. Each operation produces another relation, so the operations can be combined step by step.
goals: Use set operations, products, joins, and division
Write a multi-step algebra expression and explain intermediate results

topics.title: Selection and projection
topics.definition: Selection σ keeps rows that satisfy a condition. Projection π keeps only the requested columns.
details: Selection σ keeps complete rows that satisfy a condition. Projection π keeps the requested columns; under the relational model it removes duplicate result tuples.
Use selection to answer “which rows?” and projection to answer “which attributes?” Combine them when a question asks for a few columns from matching rows.
topics.example: σprogram='CS'(STUDENT) keeps CS students. πname(σprogram='CS'(STUDENT)) returns just their names.

topics.title: Set operations and joins
topics.definition: Set operations combine compatible relations; joins connect rows whose values satisfy a relationship condition.
details: Union R ∪ S returns rows in either relation; intersection R ∩ S returns rows in both; difference R − S returns rows in R but not S. These operations require union-compatible relations.
A theta join uses a comparison condition; an equijoin uses equality; a natural join matches same-named attributes and keeps one copy of the join column.
A Cartesian product pairs every row of one relation with every row of another. A join can be understood as a product followed by a selection.
topics.example: If CS_STUDENT and DBMS_STUDENT have compatible columns, their intersection returns students in both sets. Joining ENROLLMENT with COURSE on cid adds the course title to each registration.

topics.title: Division: 'for every'
topics.definition: Division returns values on one side that are paired with every required value on the other side.
details: It is useful when the question contains words such as 'all required courses' or 'every project part'.
To use it, compare the pairs a person has with the complete set they must have.
topics.example: ENROLLMENT(sid,cid) ÷ REQUIRED(cid) returns students enrolled in every required course.

topics.title: Renaming and Cartesian product
topics.definition: Renaming ρ gives a relation or its attributes temporary names. Cartesian product pairs every row from one relation with every row from another.
details: Renaming is especially useful when the same relation is used twice, such as comparing two employees in EMPLOYEE.
A product of relations with m and n rows has m×n row pairs before a condition filters it. Products can become large, so a join condition is normally applied.
topics.example: Rename EMPLOYEE as E1 and E2. A condition E1.managerId=E2.empId can compare an employee with a manager stored in the same relation.

topics.title: Relational algebra: a multi-step query example
topics.definition: A relational algebra expression can combine selection, join, and projection to answer one question from several tables.
details: Translate the question into three decisions: which rows qualify, which relations must be connected, and which columns belong in the answer.
Apply selective conditions early when possible. Each intermediate result is a relation and becomes the input to the next operation.
topics.example: Question: list names of CS students enrolled in DBMS. Select CS students and the DBMS course, join those results with ENROLLMENT on sid and cid, then project the student name: πname(σprogram='CS' and title='DBMS'(STUDENT ⋈ ENROLLMENT ⋈ COURSE)).

worked.title: Keep CS students, then show only their names
worked.setup: The table has three students. We want the names of the students in CS.

steps.title: Keep matching rows
steps.body: Look down the Program column. Keep Asha and Chen because their program is CS.

steps.title: Keep the needed column
steps.body: The question asks for names, so remove the ID and Program columns from the answer.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.body: The answer is Asha and Chen. In relational algebra, selection chooses rows and projection chooses columns.

worked.answer: The result is the names Asha and Chen: first select CS rows, then project the Name column.

diagram.title: A query is a chain of table operations
diagram.caption: Filter first, then choose the columns to return.

lessons.exam: Write relational-algebra expressions for selection, projection, set operations, joins, and division. Show the intermediate relation for each step.

lessons.plain: Relational calculus describes the condition a result row must satisfy. It says what to return, not which sequence of table operations to run.
goals: Tell tuple calculus from domain calculus
Explain why unsafe queries must be restricted

topics.title: Tuple relational calculus (TRC)
topics.definition: TRC uses a tuple variable to describe each possible result row. Its form is { t | condition about t }.
details: The condition can refer to tuples in relations and compare their attributes.
A tuple variable ranges over possible tuples, so a safe query must restrict it to values grounded in the database.
topics.example: {s.name | STUDENT(s) and s.program='CS'} describes the names of students whose program is CS.

topics.title: Domain relational calculus (DRC)
topics.definition: DRC uses one variable per attribute value. Its form is { <x1,…,xn> | condition about those values }.
details: TRC ranges over whole tuples; DRC ranges over the values in the tuple's columns.
Both use logic such as AND, OR, NOT, and exists. An 'all' condition can be written as 'there is no required item missing'.
topics.example: A DRC query can return <n> when some <id,n,p> is a STUDENT row and p='CS'.

topics.title: Safe queries
topics.definition: A safe query has a finite result whose values come from the active database domain.
details: A query that asks for every value that is not in a relation could range over all possible strings or numbers, producing an unbounded answer.
Make the query safe by anchoring variables to rows or values that occur in the database, then apply the negative condition.
topics.example: Instead of listing all possible people who are not students, start with the finite PERSON relation and return its rows for which no STUDENT row exists.

worked.title: Find students enrolled in DBMS
worked.setup: STUDENT has Asha (ID 1) and Bilal (ID 2). ENROLLMENT says ID 1 takes DBMS and ID 2 takes OS.

steps.title: Start with real students
steps.body: Check the students that actually appear in the STUDENT table.

steps.title: Look for a matching registration
steps.body: For each student, check ENROLLMENT for the same ID and the course DBMS.

steps.title: Return the matching name
steps.body: ID 1 has a DBMS registration, so the answer is Asha. ID 2 does not match.

worked.answer: Tuple calculus describes which student rows should be returned. Domain calculus describes which individual column values should be returned. Both express the same request: Asha.

lessons.exam: Compare TRC and DRC. Define safety and explain why an unrestricted negated query may be unsafe.

lessons.plain: Logical design turns the data model into tables. SQL can create, query, alter, and remove tables and views; a view is a saved query that can present a useful window onto data.
goals: Translate an ER design into relation schemas
Create, query, alter, and remove tables and views
Explain what a view exposes and when it can be updated

topics.title: Ask a question with SELECT
topics.definition: SELECT names the output columns; FROM names the input relations; WHERE filters rows.
details: JOIN matches related rows from different tables. GROUP BY forms groups, then COUNT, AVG, MIN, and MAX summarize each group.
ORDER BY is needed when the answer must appear in a particular order.
topics.example: SELECT cid, AVG(score) FROM Result GROUP BY cid returns one average per course.

topics.title: Create and modify database structures
topics.definition: CREATE TABLE defines columns, types, keys, and constraints. ALTER TABLE changes a table's structure.
details: CREATE TABLE defines columns, types, keys, and constraints. ALTER TABLE changes the structure; DROP TABLE removes the table definition and its stored rows.
INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes values, and DELETE removes selected rows. These are data changes, not table-structure changes.
A primary-key or foreign-key constraint is part of the schema, so the DBMS can reject invalid changes.
topics.example: Use ALTER TABLE Enrollment ADD COLUMN grade CHAR(2) to add a column. Use UPDATE Enrollment SET grade='A' WHERE sid=22 AND cid=301 to change a row; these commands affect different layers.

topics.title: Views and updatability
topics.definition: A view is a named SELECT statement. It is often updatable when each view row maps clearly to one base-table row.
details: A simple view over one table may allow updates. A grouped, aggregate, or many-table view can be ambiguous: one displayed row may represent many source rows.
Views simplify repeated queries and can limit which columns a user sees. Access permissions still decide who may read or change base data.
topics.example: A fee-summary view can show sid and balance while hiding private contact details.

topics.title: Additional SQL forms (extension)
topics.definition: These useful SQL features are not named in the official Unit 2 syllabus, so treat them as optional background after the listed topics. Triggers respond to events; embedded or dynamic SQL connects queries with programs; recursive queries follow repeated relationships.
details: A trigger runs automatically after a specified database event. Embedded SQL is written inside another programming language; dynamic SQL is assembled while a program runs.
A recursive query repeatedly follows a relationship such as an employee-manager chain. Exact syntax varies between SQL systems.
topics.example: A trigger can record an audit row after a salary update. A recursive query can follow manager_id repeatedly to find all levels above an employee.

topics.title: Drop and alter tables and views
topics.definition: ALTER changes an existing database object. DROP removes an object definition; dropping a table removes its table data as well, while dropping a view removes the saved query definition.
details: ALTER TABLE can add, remove, or change columns and constraints; exact syntax depends on the SQL system. CREATE VIEW defines a saved query, and DROP VIEW removes that view.
Some systems support ALTER VIEW or CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW to change a view definition. Other systems require dropping and recreating it.
RESTRICT blocks removal when dependent objects exist. CASCADE may remove dependent objects too, so use it only when those dependencies are intended to go.
topics.example: Examples: ALTER TABLE Enrollment ADD COLUMN grade CHAR(2); DROP VIEW CurrentStudents; DROP TABLE OldEnrollment. DROP TABLE removes the table and its rows, so check dependencies and backups first.

worked.title: Create a simple view and add a column
worked.setup: STUDENT has ID, Name, and Program. We want a saved list of CS student names, then we want to add a Phone column.

steps.title: Choose what the view shows
steps.body: The view keeps only Name and only rows where Program is CS. It acts like a saved filter.

steps.title: See the view's result
steps.body: The view shows Asha and Chen. The original STUDENT table still keeps all three rows.

steps.title: Change the table plan
steps.body: Adding a Phone column changes the table's design. Existing student rows can then be filled with phone numbers.

worked.answer: A view is a saved way to look at selected table data. Altering a table changes its columns; it does not mean deleting the whole table.

diagram.title: How a grouped query is evaluated
diagram.caption: Rows are filtered if needed, grouped by course, then summarized.
